Spring Cannabis Guide: Uplifting Strains, Bright Terpenes and Easy Formats

Why bright, citrusy strains appeal as the days get longer, what research does and doesn't say about cannabis and mood, and how to enjoy spring responsibly.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20269 min read

09min readShopping & Reviews
In this article
  1. The Winter-to-Spring Mood Shift, and When to Talk to a Doctor
  2. Cannabinoids and Mood: What's Known
  3. Do Sativa and Indica Labels Predict Mood?
  4. Terpenes People Link With an Upbeat Feel: Limonene, Pinene and Terpinolene
  5. Classic Uplifting Cannabis Strains to Look For
  6. Spring Formats: Pre-Rolls, Vapes, Low-Dose Gummies and Drinks
  7. Enjoying Spring Outdoors, Legally
  8. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Longer spring days lift many people, but seasonal depression is a medical condition to discuss with a health care provider.
  • Research reviews find scarce evidence that cannabis improves depression, and heavy use is linked to a higher risk of developing it.
  • Indica and sativa tags say little about how a strain will feel; dose, THC, CBD and terpenes say more.
  • People often describe citrusy, piney strains such as Super Lemon Haze, Jack Herer and Durban Poison as bright and uplifting.
  • Keep spring plans legal: no public use, no driving after consuming and no cannabis on federal land.

Uplifting cannabis strains are the bright, citrusy and piney ones many adults reach for as Michigan thaws out: Super Lemon Haze, Jack Herer, Durban Poison and Tangie are familiar examples. How any strain feels depends on your dose, your body and your setting, and cannabis is no substitute for care if winter has left you truly low. Below, you'll find the seasonal mood shift, where to get real help and what research says about cannabis and mood. After that come the terpenes people link with a brighter high, classic strains to look for and formats that suit a spring day.

The Winter-to-Spring Mood Shift, and When to Talk to a Doctor

Michigan winters are long and gray, and plenty of people notice their energy and outlook improve as the days stretch out in March and April. Lighter evenings, warmer air and the first patio afternoon of the year all help.

For some people, winter brings more than the blues. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes seasonal affective disorder (SAD) as a type of depression with a recurrent seasonal pattern. Its symptoms typically last about four to five months a year. The options NIMH lists are light therapy, psychotherapy, antidepressant medication and vitamin D, used alone or together. It advises talking with a health care provider about the benefits and risks of each.

Cannabis isn't on that list. If your mood has been low for weeks, or it's getting in the way of work, sleep or relationships, talk to your doctor before anything else. If you are struggling or thinking about suicide, or someone close to you is, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.

Our article on cannabis and depression looks at that research in more depth. This guide is about enjoying spring as an adult, not about managing a health condition.

Cannabinoids and Mood: What's Known

THC causes the high, and euphoria and relaxation are among the effects people describe most often. Those effects depend heavily on dose. In a lab study of healthy adults, a 12.5 mg oral dose of THC raised negative mood before and during a stressful task. A 7.5 mg dose didn't. More isn't better when the goal is a pleasant afternoon.

The longer-term picture is less rosy. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that evidence for cannabinoids improving depressive disorders or symptoms is scarce, and THC raised the rate of adverse events compared with placebo. A 2014 meta-analysis of long-term studies found that cannabis use, particularly heavy use, may be linked to a higher risk of developing depression. Its authors noted that the studies varied widely in what they controlled for, so the link isn't proof of cause.

CBD, the non-intoxicating cannabinoid, gets plenty of attention, but the same 2019 review found few randomized trials testing it for mental health conditions.

What it means for you: a pleasant high and better mental health aren't the same thing. Keep doses modest and take breaks. Check with a clinician first if you're on any medication, pregnant or breastfeeding, or living with a mental health condition.

Do Sativa and Indica Labels Predict Mood?

Dispensary shorthand says sativas energize and indicas relax, but the genetics don't back that up. In 2021, researchers who genotyped over 100 cannabis samples found no genome-wide genetic split between the sativa-labeled and indica-labeled plants. The labels lined up instead with a small number of terpenes.

In practice, the label is at best a hint about aroma. Three things predict your experience better:

  • Dose. The same strain can feel bright at a small dose and foggy or anxious at a large one.
  • THC and CBD. The label's ratio hints at how strong the high will be.
  • Terpenes and your own notes. Track which aromas you enjoy and how each strain felt.

Terpenes People Link With an Upbeat Feel: Limonene, Pinene and Terpinolene

Terpenes are the aroma compounds that make lemony strains smell like lemons and piney strains smell like a forest. Many shoppers associate three of them with a brighter, more upbeat experience:

  • Limonene brings citrus peel and shows up in many lemon- and orange-named strains. Our limonene guide covers it in depth.
  • Pinene carries the scent of a pine forest and fresh rosemary.
  • Terpinolene is herbal, floral and a little citrusy, and it's often reported as dominant in Jack Herer and Durban Poison.

You'll see limonene and pinene marketed as mood-boosting terpenes, but the evidence in people is thin. In one small 2024 study, researchers gave 20 healthy adults vaporized THC with and without limonene. When the largest limonene dose was added to the top THC dose, in a session 12 of them completed, volunteers rated themselves less anxious or nervous and less paranoid than with that THC dose alone. Limonene by itself felt no different from a placebo. That's one small study of one dose combination, not proof that a lemony strain will brighten your day. Think of terpenes as a guide to aromas you enjoy.

Some brands list terpene percentages on the package or in an online lab report; others only describe the aroma. Limonene strains tend to carry lemon, orange or tangerine in their names, but a name isn't a lab result. Your nose is a fair guide, too: if a jar's smell appeals to you, note the strain and the batch.

Classic Uplifting Cannabis Strains to Look For

These names come up often when people describe a bright, daytime high, and they fill most lists of happy strains. Lineage is as commonly listed, and effects are what people commonly report; both vary with the grower, the batch and the person.

StrainCommonly listed parentsAroma
Super Lemon HazeSuper Silver Haze × Lemon SkunkLemon peel, sweet citrus
Jack HererHaze × Northern Lights #5 × Shiva SkunkPine, spice, citrus
Durban PoisonSouth African landraceSweet, earthy, herbal
TangieCalifornia Orange × SkunkTangerine
ClementineTangie × Lemon SkunkSweet orange, lemon
Blue DreamBlueberry × HazeSweet berry, herbal

Super Lemon Haze, from the Dutch breeder Green House Seeds, is all citrus and often described as energetic and cheerful. Jack Herer and Durban Poison are terpinolene-forward classics that people call clear-headed and lively. Tangie and its offspring Clementine are the orange-peel picks. Blue Dream is the gentler option, which many people find balanced rather than racy.

Two cautions. Haze-family strains can feel racy or anxious at higher doses, so start with less than you would of a familiar strain. And names are examples, not promises: read the label's THC, CBD and test date for the batch in front of you. Our guide to energizing cannabis strains has more daytime ideas.

Spring Formats: Pre-Rolls, Vapes, Low-Dose Gummies and Drinks

Spring days are long, and an easy-to-portion format keeps things simple to manage.

FormatOnsetWhy people choose it in springKeep in mind
Pre-rollsWithin minutesSimple and shareable on a porch or patioSmoke only where it's allowed
VapesWithin minutesLess lingering smell, easy to take one small puffWait 10 minutes or more between puffs
Low-dose gummiesMuch slowerEasy to portion, nothing to lightWait well before taking more
DrinksVaries by productEasy to sip at a backyard get-togetherServings per can vary, so read the label

Pre-rolls. Mini pre-rolls keep portions small. Light up only on private property where smoking is allowed.

Vapes. A vape is quick and discreet. Take one small puff and give it at least 10 minutes before deciding on another.

Low-dose gummies. An edible starts working far more slowly than a pre-roll or vape, and it lasts longer too. Take one low-dose serving and wait well before having more. Michigan caps adult-use edible servings at 10 mg of THC, and lower-dose options make it easy to start small.

Drinks. Pace a THC drink the way you would a cocktail, and don't mix the two.

For a seasonal look at product types, see our guide to spring cannabis products.

Enjoying Spring Outdoors, Legally

Spring pulls everyone outside, but public places are off-limits for cannabis use under Michigan law, and landlords and property managers can prohibit smoking or use on their property. A few ways to keep a sunny day legal and easy:

  • Keep it at home, whether that's the porch or the backyard, or on private property where you've been given the okay.
  • Don't use cannabis behind the wheel of a car, boat, snowmobile or off-road vehicle, and never drive after consuming. Plan a sober ride instead.
  • Visiting Sleeping Bear Dunes, a national forest or other federal land? Leave cannabis behind: federal law governs there, and Michigan's law won't protect you.
  • Keep products sealed and out of reach when you travel, and away from kids and pets at home.

Plenty of spring plans pair well with a low dose on private property:

  • planting the garden or tidying the yard
  • a backyard grill-out with friends who are also 21 or older
  • a porch and a playlist on the first warm evening
  • a movie at home with the windows open

Our guide to where you can smoke in Michigan covers the details. Questions about reading a label? Stop by any of our Michigan dispensary locations and ask a budtender.

Spring cannabis is for adults 21 and older. Enjoy it responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

What strains are the most uplifting?

No strain affects everyone the same way, but people often describe citrusy, piney strains such as Super Lemon Haze, Jack Herer, Durban Poison and Tangie as bright and energetic. Dose matters as much as the strain: a small amount of something you enjoy usually feels better than a large amount of anything.

Should I use cannabis for seasonal depression?

No. Seasonal affective disorder is a type of depression, and NIMH lists light therapy, psychotherapy, antidepressant medication and vitamin D among the options to discuss with a health care provider. Reviews of the research have turned up scarce evidence that cannabinoids improve depression. If you're struggling, talk to your doctor, or call or text 988 in a crisis.

Which terpene is linked to a good mood?

Limonene, the citrus terpene, is the usual answer, with pinene and terpinolene close behind. Evidence in people is thin: one small 2024 study found limonene lowered anxious and paranoid feelings from a high THC dose, but that doesn't mean a lemony strain will lift your mood. Use terpenes to find aromas you enjoy.

Is sativa better for mood?

Not reliably. When researchers compared the genetics of sativa- and indica-labeled samples in 2021, they found no real genome-wide difference, only differences in a few aroma compounds. Your dose, the product's THC and CBD, and its terpenes say more about how it may feel. Keep notes on each strain and start low with anything new.

What's a good low-dose product for a sunny spring day?

Something easy to portion: a single low-dose gummy or drink, a mini pre-roll or one small puff from a vape. Start with the smallest serving, wait before having more, and plan to be at home or on private property with permission, not at a park or behind the wheel.

Sources

  1. National Institute of Mental Health: Seasonal Affective Disorder (revised 2023)nimh.nih.gov
  2. Black N. et al., Cannabinoids for the treatment of mental disorders and symptoms of mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Lancet Psychiatry (2019)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  3. Lev-Ran S. et al., The association between cannabis use and depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies, Psychological Medicine (2014)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  4. Childs E., Lutz J.A., de Wit H., Dose-related effects of delta-9-THC on emotional responses to acute psychosocial stress, Drug and Alcohol Dependence (2017)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  5. Watts S. et al., Cannabis labelling is associated with genetic variation in terpene synthase genes, Nature Plants (2021)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  6. Spindle T.R. et al., Vaporized D-limonene selectively mitigates the acute anxiogenic effects of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol in healthy adults who intermittently use cannabis, Drug and Alcohol Dependence (2024)pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
